*Mycoplasma* are **free living** and not obligate intracellular parasites.

They are the smallest free living microorganisms and most pleomorphic.

They are characterized by the **absence of a peptidoglycan cell wall** and resulting resistance to many antibacterial agents.

They even lack cell wall precursors like muramic acid or diaminopimelic acid.

Cells are bounded by trilaminar unit membrane containing sterols.

***Mycoplasma pneumoniae* are the only bacterial cells that possess cholesterol in their cell membrane** (obtained from the host) and possess more genes that encode for **membrane lipoprotein.**

**Lipoprotein/peptide** is able to modulate the host immune system, whose N-terminal structure is an important factor in inducing immunity.

*Mycoplasma* is non-motile but show **gliding slow movements.**

question_stem.markdown: All of the following statements are true about "L forms" except _______.

options.text: They are named after Lister institute.
They may not initiate disease similar to protoplasts and spheroplasts.
They were discovered by studying cultures of Mycoplasma.

peer_accuracy_statement: 17% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
L forms were not discovered by studying cultures of mycoplasma.

Kleinberger found Pleuropneumonia-like forms in a culture of **"Streptobacillus moniliformis."**

These were named L forms after **Lister institute, London.**

It was subsequently shown that many bacteria, either spontaneously or induced by certain substances like penicillin, lost part or all of their cell wall and develop into L forms.

**Cell wall-deficient forms** (L forms, protoplasts, spheroplasts) **may not initiate a disease** but may be important in bacterial persistence during antibiotic therapy and subsequent recurrence of infection.

They can grow and divide but they are difficult to cultivate and usually require a medium that is solidified with agar as well as having the right osmotic strength.

Internationally marketed meningococcal polysaccharide vaccines are bivalent (A and C), trivalent (A, C and W-135) or tetravalent (A, C, Y and W-135).

**Stuart transport medium** is recommended for the preservation and transportation of ***Neisseria*** species and other fastidious organisms from the clinic to the laboratory.

**Composition of Stuart medium:**

• Sodium glycerophosphate
• Sodium thioglycollate
• Calcium chloride
• Methylene blue
• Agar

This medium is a chemically defined, **semisolid, non-nutrient medium,** which prevents microbial proliferation.

Because of this composition the medium ensures that microorganisms present are able to survive for a sufficiently long period of time.

**Sodium thioglycollate** produces a reduced environment so as to improve the recovery of anaerobes.

**Methylene blue** acts as **oxidation reduction indicator.**

**Calcium chloride** maintains permeability of bacterial cells and **sodium glycerophosphate** maintains the pH of the medium

The medium appears **colorless in the reduced state** and **blue in the oxidized state.**

question_stem.markdown: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is caused by

peer_accuracy_statement: 94% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
**Waterhouse-Friderichsen Syndrome** also known as **hemorrhagic adrenalitis** or **fulminant meningococcemia** is a complication seen in infection with **N.meningitidis,** characterized by **bilateral adrenal gland hemorrhage.**

**CLINICAL PICTURE**

• Onset of the syndrome is dramatically sudden.
• Nonspecific with **fever** (initially moderate, then high), rigors, cough, vomiting, and headache.
• **Dysphagia, atrophy** of the tongue, and cracks at the corners of the mouth are also characteristic features.
• Soon a **rash** appears; first macular, and rapidly becoming petechial and purpuric with a dusky gray color and sometimes large purpuric cutaneous haemorrhages often followed by necrosis and sloughing.
• Exhibits a **cyanotic pallor,** patients are alert but pale with coldness and cyanosis of the extremities due to generalized vasoconstriction.

**COMPLICATIONS**

• **Shock,** extensive haemorrhage within the skin and fall into coma.
• Death usually after a few hours, **adrenal insufficiency** being the immediate cause.
• Patients who recover may suffer from **extensive sloughing of the skin** and loss of digits due to **gangrene**

**TREATMENT**

• The treatment is as that for meningococcal infection, fulminant meningococcemia is a **medical emergency** and needs to be treated with adequate antibiotics as fast as possible.
• **Ceftriaxone** is an antibiotic commonly employed today. Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic. Like other third- generation cephalosporins, it has broad spectrum activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.

• **Pelvic inflammatory disease** and **salpingitis** may lead to sterility.
• Rarely peritonitis may develop with perihepatic inflammation **(Fitz Hugh Curtis syndrome)**

Usual **incubation period** is 2-7 days

**Acute urethritis** is the **most common** clinical manifestation of **gonorrhea** in males and major symptoms are **urethral discharge** and **dysuria,** usually without urinary frequency or urgency.

**About Other Options**

• **Third-generation cephalosporins** have remained highly effective as **single-dose therapy** for gonorrhoea.
  ◦ Ceftriaxone (250mg, IM) single dose + treatment for chlamydia if chlamydial infection is not ruled out (Azithromycin 1 g PO, single dose or Doxycycline 100 mg PO bid for 7 days)
• Adult vagina is resistant to Gonococcus, so infection is **less severe in female.**
• In males, it can involve rectum and prostate and epididymitis. **(never involve testes).**

Note: Rising MICs of cefixime worldwide have led the CDC to discontinue its recommendation of this agent as first-line treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhea.

peer_accuracy_statement: 54% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
Ciprofloxacin is used for chemoprophylaxis of meningococcal meningitis for close contacts. Ceftriaxone and Rifampicin are also used.

Antibiotic chemoprophylaxis among close contacts of a patient with invasive meningococcal disease is recommended to prevent secondary cases.

Rifampin was earlier used widely, but it was found that it is not the optimal agent due to high risk of adverse events, emerging resistance, and the need of compliance for four doses.

Ciprofloxacin is now widely used as a single oral dose, but it cannot be given in pregnancy and those below 18 years of age.

In pregnancy and in all ages, ceftriaxone can be given, as a single IM or IV dose. However, reduced susceptibility of isolates to Ceftriaxone has occasionally been reported.

Icosahedron has 20 faces and 12 vertices.

The filamentous viral nucleic acid–protein complex (nucleo capsid) is then coiled inside a lipid-containing envelope. A regular, periodic interaction between capsid protein and nucleic acid is required to maintain a stable helical symmetry. Therefore, it is **not possible for empty helical particles to form.**

images.visual_description: Photograph of a circular culture plate containing a purple/violet-stained cell monolayer dotted with numerous small, discrete, unstained white circular zones of cell lysis (viral plaques caused by Herpes simplex virus).

explanation_markdown:
Quantitative infectivity assay of viruses is done by plaque assay.

**Assay of infectivity:** There are two types of infectivity assays:

A) Quantitative: measure the actual number of infectious particles in the inoculum

B) Quantal assays: only indicate the presence or absence of infectious viruses

**A. Quantitative assay**

**1. Plaque assay:** Plaque-based assays are the **standard method** used to determine virus concentration in terms of infectious dose. A viral plaque is formed when a virus infects a cell within the fixed **cell monolayer.** Viral plaque assays determine the number of **plaque-forming units (pfu)** in a virus sample.

The image given below shows viral plaques caused by Herpes simplex virus.

**2. Pock assay:** In this method, the appropriately diluted viral sample is inoculated into the epithelial layer of the chorioallantoic membrane (CAM) of a chick embryo in an embryonated chicken egg.

**B. Quantal assay**

**1. End-point biologic assays:** 50% tissue culture infective dose **(TCID50)** is the measure of infectious virus titer. This is an endpoint dilution assay, which quantifies the amount of virus required to kill 50% of infected hosts or to produce a cytopathic effect in 50% of inoculated tissue culture cells.

Interferons are a family of host-coded proteins produced by cells on induction by viral or non-viral inducers.

• Species specific
• Inactivated by Proteases

pearls.body_text:

explanation_markdown:
Painful genital ulcers and painful inguinal lymph adenopathy is suggestive of herpes virus infection. The best step in the management of delivery in this patient is **Cesarean section.**

• **Herpes infection** in the newborn may occur during birth, particularly **if the mother has genital lesions due to HSV-2.** In such cases, **Cesarean section may prevent infection.**
• If neonatal herpes occurs, it may be confined to the eyes, ears, mouth, or skin, but is more commonly a disseminated infection involving multiple organs, with or without encephalitis.
• The mortality rate is very high in neonatal herpes and survivors may have neurological impairment.

So, in the above patient, cesarean section is the best management to prevent neonatal herpes infection.

peer_accuracy_statement: 25% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
**ORF virus**

The orf virus is a species of Parapoxvirus. It causes a disease in sheep and goats that is prevalent worldwide. The disease is also called contagious pustular dermatitis or sore mouth infection.

Orf is transmitted to humans by direct contact with an infected animal. **It is an occupational disease of sheep and goat handlers.** Recent reports from the United States empha- sized the temporal association between human lesions and recent flock vaccination with live orf virus. Infection by orf virus is facilitated by skin trauma. Infection of humans occurs usually as a single lesion on a finger, hand, or forearm but may appear on the face or neck. Lesions are large nodules, rather painful, with surrounding inflamed skin. The infection is seldom generalized. Healing takes several weeks.

Electron microscopy can confirm a parapoxvirus infection, but only nucleic acid testing methods can definitively identify a parapoxvirus as orf virus.

question_stem.text: Hepatitis B infection is acquired by the foetus by which of the following ways ?
question_stem.markdown: Hepatitis B infection is acquired by the foetus by which of the following ways ?

peer_accuracy_statement: 67% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
All of the above are causes for Hepatitis B infection in foetus.

Mother-to-child transmission of HBV can occur via **three modalities:** intrauterine transmission; transmission during delivery; and postpartum transmission.

**Intrauterine transmission** accounts for only a minority of cases of HBV transmission. A high viral load and positivity of HBeAg were factors associated with an increased risk of transmission through this route.

HBV can reach the fetus by crossing the placental barrier. HBV can infect and replicate in all types of placental cells before it reaches the fetus. It is noteworthy that the percent of infected cells decreases from the maternal side (43.6%) to the fetus side (18.8%) of the placenta. Finally, HBV may reach the fetus through transplacental leakage of the maternal blood into fetal circulation, a condition that is associated with prolonged threatened preterm labor or threatened abortion due to increased uterine contractions.

Transmission of HBV **during delivery** is the **most frequent method** of vertical transmission. It is mostly due to newborn contact with the mother's infected secretions or blood at the time of delivery.

**Postpartum transmission :** A proportion of babies (as high as 34%) may acquire infection after birth due to close contact with the mother. However, breastfeeding is not a risk factor for HBV infection.

Transmission following amniocentesis has been described, but the risk appears to be low.
